articles.title_orig: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.title_zh: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.content_orig:
U.S. and world health officials are calling on Russia to share more information after Russian media reports said a scientist at an infectious disease research facility in Siberia died after possibly contracting plague during a lab accident.
The reports have caused concern, even as the World Health Organization says "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low," based on the current information.
Dr. Céline Gounder, a CBS News medical contributor and editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News, echoed that belief on "CBS Mornings" on Tuesday.
"The American public does not need to be worried," she said.
Still, an official cause of death has not been made public and a lack of transparency from Russia has led some experts to question if the lab worker had the plague.
"The response doesn't fit plague. It's not congruent with plague," Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, told CBS News. "Plague is something, in the 21st century, that's treatable with antibiotics."
Russian media has reported that a female researcher, identified as Darya Shipilova, 28, died after being exposed to the plague in a lab accident at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. Initial reports said that Shipilova broke a test tube containing the plague bacteria Yersinia pestis in late September, came down with severe pneumonia and died of her illness.
The World Health Organization said Shipilova died of severe pneumonia overnight into Oct. 2.
Russian officials have since cast doubt on those reports. Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said there was no accident and that Shipilova had died of "pneumonia of unknown origin."
The WHO said it was told by Russia on Oct. 6 that no plague was detected. The global health agency said it asked Russian authorities to provide information about which pathogen caused Shipilova's illness.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called on Russia to be more transparent, and said the nation should "share more information with the world." The WHO said it is following the situation closely and requesting further information from Russian authorities.
Plague is caused by the Yersinia pestis bacteria. There are three main types of plague : bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
Bubonic plague is the most common form of plague. Infected people may have painfully swollen lymph nodes known as buboes, along with fever and chills, a severe headache, body aches and exhaustion.
Septicemic plague happens when the Yersinia pestis bacteria enters the bloodstream. Patients may develop fever, chills, extreme weakness, abdominal pain, shock and possible internal bleeding. Some skin may turn black and die.
Pneumonic plague typically occurs when the other forms of plague are not treated and the Yersinia pestis bacteria infects the lungs. Patients develop pneumonia and may show fever, headache, weakness, shortness of breath, chest pain, cough and bloody or watery mucus. The pneumonia could cause respiratory failure. This is considered the most serious version of plague, and is always fatal if left untreated.
Russian media reports indicated that Shipilova may have died of pneumonic plague.
Plague is most commonly spread through the bite of fleas carried by infected rodents. Animals, including cats and dogs, can also become infected from eating smaller animals that were carrying those fleas.
Pneumonic plague can be spread between people. In cases of pneumonic plague, droplets emitted when a sick person coughs can lead to others becoming infected.
Russia's health watchdog said that nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova before her death were tested, and none had plague.
Plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics, health organizations and doctors say. Patients need to be treated as soon as possible.
Researchers who regularly work with plague can also be vaccinated for it, Gounder noted.
Plague outbreaks in the Middle Ages killed millions, due to widespread, common flea and rat infestations and less understanding of how to prevent disease from spreading.
About seven plague cases are reported each year in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . More than 80% of the cases in the U.S. are bubonic plague, the agency said.
Most U.S. cases occur in the West and Southwest. Cases are usually treated successfully, according to CDC data. The last fatal case of plague in the U.S. was recorded in 2021.

Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief has been detained on suspicion of passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the country’s federal prosecutor’s office has said.
Prosecutors allege August Hanning, whose tenure at the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) ended in 2005, paid for access to classified documents from a former aide at the BND. It is claimed Hanning used them to prepare an analysis which he intended to sell on to a foreign intelligence service as part of his consulting activities.
He is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason and espionage”, the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Prosecutors did not identify which foreign intelligence service he was allegedly preparing the analysis for, and it ⁠was not immediately clear whether it reached its intended recipient.
According to German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung the case does not ⁠involve Russia.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Tölz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany on Tuesday. The former aide, ‌identified only as Manfred D, was also arrested on Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany.
Manfred D is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Prosecutors said they are also searching the suspects’ premises in these locations and in Berlin.
From the spring of 2010 until July 2022, Manfred D continuously obtained valuable information for Hanning from the BND in exchange for payment, said the prosecutor’s statement.
He allegedly provided him with nearly 2,000 documents, many of them classified and intended solely for internal use within the BND and senior-level intelligence ‌briefings at the chancellery.
According to the statement, Hanning was in close contact with a member of another state intelligence service, and he supplied this individual with political information over several years, which was partly based on material he had received from Manfred D.
Hanning was president of the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. Manfred D served as his chief of staff at that time, and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
“In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor's office said.
The German newspaper Bild said that the investigation was launched after the discovery of an alleged leak of intelligence reports intended for the chancellery.
The arrests came after a separate investigation into allegations that Hanning abducted Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.
The current investigation stems from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
Both of the accused will be brought before the investigating judge of the Federal Court of Justice on Tuesday and Wednesday.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz voiced his shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
“This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
“We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations levelled against former BND chief Hanning,” von Notz told Spiegel Online.

Agents arrested August Hanning (pictured from 2015) at his home on Tuesday
Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.
Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near MÃ¼nster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.
Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.
"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".
Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".
Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.
Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.
State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.
It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.

A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges after an investigation into a surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 children ranging in age from a few months to 13 years, authorities said Tuesday.
Guojun Xuan, 66, and his wife, Silvia Zhang, 39, face several counts of child abuse, as well as conspiracy to commit child abuse, accessory after the fact, and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said.
“This case is unprecedented. It is horrific,” Hochman said during a news conference Tuesday morning. “The physical abuse, beating and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.”
Prosecutors are seeking $100 million bail for the couple because of the serious nature of the charges and because they are flight risks, Hochman said. They were scheduled to be arraigned at the Pasadena courthouse later Tuesday.
Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from 2 months to 13 years, with most between 1 and 3. Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children while the rest were carried and delivered by surrogates.
Hochman said the couple set up a surrogacy agency that they operated from their home and used that agency to hire surrogates throughout the U.S.
“The house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredible young children,” Hochman said.
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their 2-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of a nanny at the home violently shaking the baby, according to Arcadia police.
Arcadia police did not file charges at the time, saying they needed to complete the investigation.
Hochman said the couple set up three rooms they called learning centers, where the children spent several hours a day sitting at desks under the supervision of nannies.
Through an extensive surveillance system including motion-activated cameras, the couple watched as the nannies subjected the children to physical abuse including daily beatings, he said.
In one video, Xuan enters one of the rooms and tells a nanny to strike a child harder, and in another he joins the nanny in hitting the child, Hochman said.
He said the nannies were told “not to leave any physical marks on the children,” and when police arrived to investigate in May 2025, the couple told the children to deny they had been beaten.
After examining the surveillance footage, police issued an arrest warrant for Chunmei Li, the nanny seen hurting the 2-month-old infant, but she could not be found.
Hochman said “there will be a reckoning” for the defendants, one of whom faces more than 17 years in prison if convicted.
When asked about the couple’s motivation, Hochman said that was part of the ongoing investigation, as was the parentage of each child.
Mitchell Krems, Xuan’s attorney, previously told ABC7 that Xuan’s goal was to raise children who become productive adults.
“The reason he has all these children is because he wants them to contribute to society. He is not a man who is self-indulgent,” Krems said. “Some who are wealthy might spend on jewelry or cars, but he is actually spending his resources to help his children become educated so that they can be the philosophers, the physicians, the researchers and the inventors that help society.”
Krems did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment on Tuesday’s arrests.
Surrogacy is an arrangement in which a woman agrees to carry and deliver a child for another person or couple, often after an embryo transfer.
There is no comprehensive federal law regulating surrogacy, leaving most rules to the states.
California is considered a “surrogacy-friendly state” because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
Investigators have said they were looking into whether the couple had misled surrogates around the country and that at least eight women came forward to say they were aggressively pursued by the couple to serve as surrogates.
The women, many of whom were first-time surrogates, say they were given misleading or incomplete information about the couple’s family situation and intentions.
At least one, Kayla Elliott, is now trying to get custody of a baby she birthed for the couple.

articles.title_orig: Toyota shuts down rumors claiming that it’s ‘slashing prices’ in China
articles.title_zh: Toyota shuts down rumors claiming that it’s ‘slashing prices’ in China
articles.content_orig:
Toyota’s joint venture, FAW Toyota, issued a statement denying reports that it’s “slashing prices” in China and may exit the market entirely.
Toyota sells vehicles in China through two joint ventures: FAW Toyota and GAC Toyota. The long-standing joint ventures produce and sell Toyota models, including the Corolla, RAV4, and Avalon, as well as new electric vehicles like the bZ3 and bZ5.
Last week, on September 28, GAC Group announced plans to acquire a 50% stake in FAW Toyota. The plans include issuing new A-shares priced at 5.75 yuan per share.
Under the agreement, GAC said that FAW Group would become its second-largest shareholder, but exact details would be finalized following an audit and once the valuation work was complete.
FAW Toyota was established in 2000 as a joint venture between FAW Group and Toyota, with each holding a 50% share. It was initially called Tianjin FAW Toyota Motor Co until 2003, when it adopted the name FAW Toyota.
Once the agreement is finalized, GAC Group would take FAW’s 50% stake, while Toyota would retain the other 50%. GAC said the deal would not change the controller.
The move was widely viewed as part of Toyota’s efforts to revamp slumping brand sales in China and streamline operations.
Since the announcement, several reports have claimed that FAW Toyota plans to exit the market completely and is slashing prices to sell down inventory.
FAW Toyota issued a statement on Monday night, refuting the false claims. The company said:
In response to false statements circulating on certain online platforms —such as claims that “FAW Toyota may completely exit the market” and “Toyota is slashing prices”—our company reserves the right to pursue legal action.
The joint venture added that “the production, sales, and iterative development plans for all models are progressing smoothly as scheduled.”
Looking ahead, FAW Toyota will leverage the Group’s broader resources and technology for upcoming vehicles.
Toyota’s sales in China fell by 22.8% in August, marking the seventh straight month of lower sales due to weak demand for gas and hybrid models amid soaring fuel prices.

articles.title_orig: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.title_zh: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.content_orig:
YANKTON, S.D. – Julie Jones won silver at the World Archery 3D Championships, and in doing so created history by becoming the first USA woman to win an individual medal at the event, which began in 2003.
Jones was making only her second-ever appearance at the World Archery 3D Championships. She was part of the women’s team including Jayme Buchanan, Katherine Li and Madison Ritter to claim bronze at the 2024 World 3D Championships in Mokrice, Slovenia. Two years on and she did even better.
“It's a little surreal, I'll be honest,” began Julie Jones on hearing she had made history. “I love 3D. That is my passion aside from hunting. I guess if you ask me how I felt about it, I'm glad that I could bring it back for the U.S. team. But it really isn't a short answer. It goes a lot further than that.
"This whole time that I've been shooting, I've had an incredible team of people behind me from the very beginning. They have encouraged, they've pushed, they've believed in me when I had doubts about my own abilities. Without them, none of none of this would have been possible.
“I know that I don't have to prove anything to them but bringing this silver medal home, it's a testament to the training and the coaching that that I've received, that this medal belongs to all of these people, not just to me.”
Jones was seeded seventh after qualification before moving through the bracket with wins over teammate Mandy Boggs, Olga Timofeeva (RUS) and Martina Blahusova (CZE). The U.S. archer from Texas settled for silver after defeat in the gold medal match to fifth seed Judith Wenzl (GER).
“I had 100 percent confidence in the training and the coaching that I'd received," explained Jones. "I knew that if I applied all of the mental work, all of the physical work, as well as the actual shooting, I was reasonably confident that I could be in the top 10. That really wasn't a doubt in my mind.
"I knew that if I ran my process and executed well, that there was a good chance I would be in the top five, if not the top three. So that part of it was not necessarily a surprise to me.
“I've had some health challenges along the way and so day two was not a good day for me physically. And it was a struggle just to make it through the round. So that kind of threw a spanner into it.
“But I'm glad that it worked out as well as it did. I shoot very well under pressure. And I knew that if I could make it into those head-to-head eliminations, that I could work. Even though I had dropped points on day two, I knew that I could work myself back up to a to a better position.”
Julie Jones was also part of the bronze medal-winning traditional mixed team alongside Cody Hasson. Hasson, a double gold medalist at last year’s Pan American Field Championships, finished sixth in the individual men’s event.
Jones added, “I am tickled to death that Cody and I ended up with the bronze medal. He is a really, really strong shooter. I may be mistaken, but I don't think he's ever medaled before (at World 3D), and just to see the excitement and the absolute joy on his and our coach Shiloh's (Butts) face, when we realized that we had won that last round, that was a great feeling.”
For Jones, this was a family affair, with husband Daniel having also made the team. For Daniel, it was not only his World 3D Championship debut but also his first major event outside of local competition. A first major event for Daniel and the first U.S. woman to win an individual medal at the World 3D Championships for Julie. A case of keeping up with the Joneses!
“I'm just a normal person,” continued Julie. “I'm a mom. I have kids. I'm self-employed. I don't have a big, fancy facility, but, you know, I go out and I'm passionate about 3D archery.”
This success comes just a few weeks before a significant birthday for Julie on November 1. She said with a smile, “Just a month before, to achieve this, I couldn’t ask for anything more. This is year 50 for me. I have my 50th birthday coming up. And winning individual silver is pretty much the best present that I could imagine.”
Matt Hudson and Ava Jones combined to take silver in the barebow mixed team. Seeded at number two, the pair defeated Austria (150-136) and Denmark (152-141) before defeat to Russia (144-123). Ava Jones, making her World Archery 3D Championships debut, came in fourth in barebow women.
Other top 10 individual finishes came for Kim Timberlake (4th in longbow women), Joella Bates (8th in longbow women) and Lee Wilkins (10th in longbow men). Timberlake’s march to the bronze medal match included a 96-66 quarterfinals win over third seed Paula Virmasalo (FIN).

articles.title_zh: Inside Christina Zhu’s strategy for Walmart’s $24.6 billion China business

China represents just 3% of Walmart’s business. But the market is fast-growing—and in charge of that growth is Christina Zhu, the president and CEO of Walmart China.
Zhu is one of the execs featured on Fortune’s new Most Powerful Women Asia list , published today. She comes in at No. 19 for her role running a $24.6 billion business that has grown 19% year-over-year.
My colleague Nicholas Gordon writes about Zhu’s tenure in the role and Walmart’s history in China in a new feature . Walmart entered China in 1996. Today, its success comes from a few strategies to meet the high expectations of the Chinese shopper: extreme convenience, in the form of lightning-fast delivery, and an “in-person shopping experience so novel that stores have become vacation destinations for shoppers throughout the region.” In China, Sam’s Club is bigger than Walmart’s namesake retailer. Shoppers show up to buy in bulk items including gift boxes of mooncakes and abalone for the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Other execs who make this year’s MPW Asia list include repeat No. 1 Tan Su Shan, who leads the Singapore-based bank DBS Group and familiar faces like Canva’s Melanie Perkins and Huawei’s Meng Wanzhou, who all appeared on our 2026 global MPW list .

articles.title_orig: The most ambitious ideas to save the world from El Niño
articles.title_zh: The most ambitious ideas to save the world from El Niño
articles.content_orig:
Countries around the world are bracing for a torrid few months as the El Niño weather phenomenon looks set to wreak havoc on shorelines, farmland and ocean ecosystems.
Already, India is grappling with the impacts of one of the driest monsoon seasons on record. Meanwhile, in Indonesia, schools have closed and authorities have advised residents to stay indoors to avoid the toxic smoke from huge wildfires supercharged by El Niño .
But what if we could take the sting out of the tail of El Niño – or even stop it from happening altogether? That’s the hope of physicists, chemists and engineers working on ideas ranging from the outrageously radical to the just-might-work.
One of the most ambitious ideas for halting El Niño is to repurpose a technique called artificial upwelling that was initially conceived to boost the uptake of carbon by the oceans. This form of geoengineering involves pumping cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean up to the surface to encourage the growth of plankton, which would then absorb and store carbon from the atmosphere.
Katharine Ricke at the University of California, San Diego, says artificial upwelling could be used to cool sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, potentially preventing an El Niño from forming .
Explainer: What is El Niño?
But – and it is a big but – the technical feasibility of deploying artificial upwelling on this scale would be a “major, major undertaking”, she says. Ricke has previously investigated whether the approach could be used to cool sea-surface temperatures in the Indian Ocean and found it would require approximately 5.8 million kilometres of pipe, nearly double the total length of all pipelines in the world.
There is also the problem that nobody knows what putting that amount of pipework into the ocean would do to other marine life. “The ecosystem effects of installing ocean pipes at that scale are really not well understood at all,” she says.
Another equally ambitious, but perhaps more promising, approach for preventing El Niño could be to use another geoengineering technique called marine cloud brightening.
The El Niño climate phase occurs when easterly winds weaken, allowing warm water built up in the western Pacific to slosh back across the central and eastern parts of the ocean. Spraying droplets of seawater into the air below low-lying stratocumulus clouds in the Pacific would increase their brightness, reflecting more sunlight back to space. This would then bring down sea-surface temperatures, strengthening trade winds to blow warm water back into the western Pacific and reverse the El Niño pattern.
A study published in July, co-authored by Ricke, concluded that deploying marine cloud brightening in this way would dramatically reduce the strength of an El Niño and push the system back into a neutral state much earlier than normal.
Why is this monster El Niño so strong?
This won’t come in time to prevent the current El Niño, says Jessica Wan at the University of Chicago, a co-author of the research. The technology needed to brighten clouds on this scale doesn’t exist, plus there is no international framework for countries to agree this kind of geoengineering intervention. “It’s not something we could implement for this El Niño or maybe even the next one,” says Wan.
So, for now at least, El Niño cycles aren’t going anywhere – but can we make them more tolerable?
One particularly devastating consequence of the way El Niño turns up the global temperature dial and shifts rain patterns around the world is that it threatens food supplies. The United Nations World Food Programme estimates that 274 million people in 45 countries will be acutely food insecure by the end of 2027, 49 million more than today.
Work is under way to develop new breeds of crops capable of withstanding the extreme conditions brought about with El Niño. Rice is a particular priority, says Erik Murchie at the University of Nottingham in the UK.
Murchie is part of a team developing heat-tolerant rice varieties, with trials now ongoing in the Philippines. This is part of a global effort: in 2025, researchers in China reported the discovery of a gene variant that can preserve yield and rice quality during hot nights, one of the major threats to rice yields. Gene-editing or selective breeding could allow this trait in commercial crops, the team says, with the field trials indicating a 31 to 78 per cent greater yield under high temperatures compared with standard rice strains.
Such a goal isn’t a fantasy – in the 1990s, scientists pinpointed a rice gene that allows a traditional rice variety known as FR13A to survive a week of submergence in flood water. The SUB1 gene has since been introduced into several major rice varieties around the world, making crops more resilient to climate-driven flood risks.
Housing, people and infrastructure are also vulnerable to rising water levels and flooding driven by El Niño. Traditional flood-protection measures are already being deployed, from coastal barricades to temporary barriers. In California, drains are being cleared and sandbags handed out, while residents are being urged to prepare their properties for high winds and flood risk.
But one company has a more drastic idea to protect against flood risk more permanently: raising the height of land. California start-up Terranova has developed a robot that injects a mix of wood slurry into the ground, raising the height of land at risk of flooding from sea-level rise.
The robots drill wells around 12 to 18 metres deep into the ground and then inject the mix, made from wood waste, into the earth. The robotic system can lift up a roughly 4000-square-metre area by about 30 centimetres per day, the firm says.  “We’re combining heavy robotics and geotechnical innovation to literally reshape the world,” the firm’s CEO Laurence Allen said in a 2025 statement announcing $7 million of venture capital investment.
However, Nigel Wright at the University of Birmingham in the UK says extensive testing should be done before deploying the technology at a large scale. He queries whether the wood waste would solidify, remain as slurry or decompose underground over the long term. “I would question whether the soil structure would be stable enough over 20 or 30 years to actually support houses,” he says.
Inside the oceans, coral reefs are on the front line of the El Niño crisis. Elevated ocean temperatures caused by El Niño can cause mass coral-bleaching events, in which corals expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissues. This process can severely stress, and ultimately kill, corals.
Shading corals could help. One test of the approach is happening this month: five floating hexagons that block harmful ultraviolet rays are being installed in a small coral nursery in Florida. The plan is to extend this to 100 shading units in June next year, which will be distributed among restoration organisations working across Florida to test their effectiveness at protecting corals and any impact on the long-term health of the ecosystem.
In Australia, an approach that goes even further has been tested. Greg Qiao at the University of Melbourne set out more than a decade ago to create a chemical film that would sit atop agricultural reservoirs to minimise water loss to evaporation. After extensive trials, that idea never came to fruition – but Qiao realised the work could be repurposed for coral reefs.
The aim for a coral reef is to block sunlight, rather than prevent evaporation, so Qiao’s team developed a thin film layer made from calcium carbonate coated with stearic acid. The layer is one molecule thick and designed to sit on the surface of the ocean above a reef. Field trials in 2018 suggested the film reduced light hitting the corals by 30 per cent. “That’s probably enough for us to stop the bleach,” says Qiao. articles.title_orig: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.title_zh: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.content_orig:
The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.
Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response.
The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached.
The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement.
According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead.
Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme, former British ambassador to Israel, Matthew Gould, said any decision by the UK to expel Israeli diplomats would inflict "grievous damage" on the relationship between both countries.
He said areas affected could include defence, security and technology.
Gould told the programme: "When you've got to a stage where you are chucking out the big majority of Israeli diplomats in London, I don't think that's purely symbolic.
"I think at that point you're doing really quite serious damage to the structure and the substructure of the relationship."
He added that governments "have a choice", that the expulsion of Israeli diplomats would be a "gift to the Israeli right", and would help Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu win re-election.
France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them.
Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution."
She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it."
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close.
"It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month.

articles.title_orig: Idaho sets new Guinness World Record for largest serving of French fries
articles.title_zh: Idaho sets new Guinness World Record for largest serving of French fries
articles.content_orig:
Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
Idaho is now home to a new Guinness World Records title after a team served up more than 1,400 pounds of french fries in Boise.
Click here for updates on this story
SOUTHEAST BOISE, Idaho ( KIVI ) -- Idaho is now home to a new Guinness World Records title after the Idaho Potato Commission and Spud Daddy served up more than 1,400 pounds of French fries Friday night.
The team was attempting to beat the previous record for the largest serving of French fries, which stood at 1,452.85 pounds and was set in India in 2018.
“Idaho should have that record,” Thomas Watson with Spud Daddy said. “Idaho doesn’t have that record, and it’s our mission to bring the record home.”
The attempt took plenty of preparation and a large group of volunteers.
Watson said about 50 to 60 people helped cut and flash-freeze the potatoes before they were loaded into a refrigerated truck and eventually fried for the final attempt.
“It’s been awesome just to see it,” Watson said.
About 1,700 pounds of raw Idaho potatoes went into the effort.
After the fries were cooked and weighed, the final total came in at 1,474 pounds — more than 20 pounds above the previous record.
That made Idaho the new Guinness World Records holder for the largest serving of French fries.
The record attempt was part of Potato Days at the Idaho Botanical Garden, a family-friendly event celebrating Idaho's potato industry and the farmers, packers, distributors and retailers behind it.
The event also featured the Big Idaho Potato Truck, live music, lawn games and plenty of potato-based food, including fries, tots, mashed potatoes, loaded baked potatoes and potato soup.
After the record was officially set, Watson said he was ready to finally relax.
“I’m ready to take a nap,” Watson said. “I’m going to be so excited that this thing we have been thinking about is now done. We can go to sleep. We can get some food. We can eat some French fries.”

Truckers could begin seeing relief from high diesel prices as soon as Saturday, Chris Wright said, after President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at temporarily expanding highway access to red-dyed diesel and providing relief from certain federal diesel-tax penalties and payments.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright joined FOX Business’ Stuart Varney on " Varney & Co. " to discuss the administration’s push to bring down diesel prices as tight global supplies continue to squeeze drivers and businesses.

"The order was signed yesterday, and it's five days for Treasury and the Department of War to find the specific authorizations."

It also directs the IRS to provide penalty relief for dyed diesel sold for highway use or used on highways through Dec. 31, while federal agencies work with states and industry to expand access.

articles.title_orig: The Email She’d Been Waiting For
articles.title_zh: The Email She’d Been Waiting For
articles.content_orig:
The Colorado State freshman had spent years working her way through New Zealand’s youth national system, hoping for an opportunity to represent her country on the world stage. Now, just weeks into her first preseason with the Rams, the opportunity was in front of her.
While typically a call, O’Brien received an email of New Zealand's roster for the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland.
“Usually we'll get an email saying, “hey, you'll get called in a week,” but we just got the straight email. I was scrolling, scrolling, scrolling. I was like, “Oh my gosh,” when I saw my name,” O’Brien said. “My best friend, who's at Xavier, she also made it and we've known each other since we were 10. It was amazing.”
Although not her typical way of being selected for a roster, it became even more special when she found her best friend of more than a decade, Penny Brill, would be joining her on the squad.
O’Brien made a quick call home followed by a message to Colorado State coach Keeley Hagen.
“I called my mom and my dad first and then I messaged Keeley, which was so exciting because she knew that I was nervous and didn't know fully, 100% if I was going,” O’Brien said. “So that was a really special moment.”
One of the highest honors awarded to a young female soccer player, this was an opportunity she built throughout her childhood. Her selection was the culmination of years spent developing with New Zealand's youth system.
O’Brien represented New Zealand at the U-17 and U-19 levels. However, after attending a camp in the U-17s, O’Brien tore a ligament in her ankle, making her unavailable just before the 2024 World Cup.
This setback did not end her World Cup ambitions as O'Brien later made New Zealand’s U-20 squad, joining them for the competition qualifier in Tahiti in 2025.
New Zealand won the Oceania tournament, securing its place in the 2026 World Cup and giving O’Brien the opportunity she had been working toward.
“That gave us qualification for the World Cup winning that, and then we were drawn in a pool, a very hard pool,” O’Brien said. “We had America, Italy, and Japan, which is basically the pool of death. But we were super excited; such a cool opportunity to play such high-class teams.”
Following the qualifier, O’Brien and the Kiwis faced off twice against Australia in a preparatory series in late May, building momentum ahead of the World Cup. Both games came up a draw, using the time for coaches to look at the quad and players to get a feel of what they might encounter in Poland. For O’Brien, it gave her more than the opportunity to wear her country’s kit, it gave her the confidence she needed to compete at a higher level and test herself.
The timing of the selection came at an unusual juncture for O’Brien. She had just begun to settle in at CSU when she learned she would soon have to leave for Poland.
As a true freshman living in the dorms, O’Brien was navigating life in a new country, a new idea of school, and the demands of a collegiate soccer player. Her new roommate and teammate, Fabienne Bos, became one of the people sharing the experience with her.
Bos remembered O’Brien discussing the possibility of making the New Zealand roster, knowing how much the opportunity meant.
“She was telling me about the World Cup coming up and she was pretty confident about making the team,” Bos said. “But of course it's always a scary, scary moment because she really wants to make it. When she made it, she was just very happy.”
Not only did O’Brien receive lots of support from her new roommate, but also from CSU’s coaching staff. They helped O’Brien prepare for the differences between an American college game and New Zealand's national system.
New Zealand’s play looks a little different than out in the West, focusing mostly on defense, something that the Rams were going to have to prepare O’Brien to face.
“Keeley and the whole team were obviously so excited for me and wanted to prepare me in the best way possible and have such a high standard of training,” O’Brien said. “I played fullback for a bit, which was helping me prepare because we play a 3-5-2 for our country, it's a little bit more defensive. Getting some experience there was really helpful before I went. Keeley did that for me, which was amazing.”
O’Brien’s journey to the World Cup was not one she made alone. CSU’s coaching staff worked to help her meet the demands of a new game.
Through on and off field training, CSU staff helped to shape O’Brien’s natural skills into something she could use anywhere.
“I sat down and went over some film with her because they were obviously really focused on the defensive side. I tell all our players, we're a resource here to help you,” Hagen said. “That was obviously unique and awesome for Poppy, and we try to help her in every way, training being one of them, film being another thing. So that's what we did.”
With much preparation from staff, O’Brien left with support which gave an opportunity to enter the World Cup more familiar with her national team’s demands.
Before the tournament began, the team faced off in a friendly against South Korea in a scoreless draw and eventually winning the penalty shootout 5-4. Additionally, the Kiwis played a professional club in Poland, using the games to prepare for the speed and physicality of World Cup competition.
“We had that time together to prepare and get back as a team after not being together for a while,” O’Brien said. “So that was really beneficial, and then straight into it, basically”
New Zealand started tournament play against Japan on Sept. 5 in Lódz, Poland. Japan dominated a scoreless first half and opened the second with a quick goal off a header from close range. New Zealand’s Lily Brazendale equalized the game only 10 minutes later with an easy tap.
The Kiwis ultimately fell 2-1 after Japan capitalized on a late penalty, breaking the stubborn New Zealand defense. The loss set the tone for a difficult group stage against three powerful opponents. New Zealand faced Italy on Sept. 9, losing 3-0, before meeting the United States on Sept.12 in a 9-0 defeat.
Although not scoring herself, O’Brien played in all three games providing New Zealand with depth and pace.
The result left New Zealand tied for 22nd place with New Caledonia and Costa Rica. Despite the losses, the Kiwis and O’Brien were grateful for the opportunity to show up on such a large stage. With 54 teams and some of the best players in the world, O’Brien still looked to the bright side.
“No matter what, I feel like representing your country is such an honor and such a pride. Compared to that U-20 level, it's just that one step up of excitement,” O’Brien said. “Playing against mostly pro players is super cool. The game's that much more physical and that much more technical, just learning so much was awesome as well.”
This experience on an international stage gave O’Brien a chance to measure herself against elite competition and take lessons back to CSU.
After the results in Poland, O’Brien still had something left unfinished and people who waited for her return. Her selection allowed her to play in Colorado State’s first two matches of the season, but it was a month before she would be a Ram again, reemerging in the lineup against Wyoming on Sept. 17. She has since started the past three matches.
Her time away from CSU had not separated her from the Rams, as her team continued to support her throughout the tournament, even catching her game against the US. Through check-ins and encouragement, the Rams showed that no matter the outcome, she still had family back in the States.
“I’m super honored for her to have that. It's the highest privilege that you can have to represent your home team; just so happy that she got that experience,” Hagen said. “We let her go and gave her what she needed. The team supported her, texted her, just tried to encourage her every step of the way.”
One of these teammates waiting to support her was her roommate.

articles.title_orig: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.title_zh: Whistleblower suit alleges Trump ordered FBI investigation on LA anti-ICE protesters
articles.content_orig:
The White House denies the allegations as ‘false’ and says the ‘first amendment does not protect violent rioting’
US politics live – latest updates
Donald Trump ordered the FBI to investigate protesters in Los Angeles who were demonstrating against the president’s immigration crackdown, according to a whistleblower complaint.
US senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat who represents California and serves on the Senate judiciary committee, said his office had received a copy of the complaint, which makes sweeping allegations about the Trump administration’s response to protests in LA in early 2025.
Demonstrators had been protesting against Trump’s deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to push the president’s agenda.
“These allegations are deeply alarming,” Padilla, who also serves as the top Democrat on the border security and immigration subcommittee, said in a statement. “Using the FBI to target Americans for exercising their first amendment rights directly undermines our nation’s foundational values. I won’t rest until we get answers.”
NBC first reported on the allegations after viewing a copy of the disclosure, which identifies the whistleblower as Jill Fields, a former supervisory intelligence analyst in the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, who made the complaint following the federal response to anti-ICE protests around the city’s federal buildings, and in residential area, in February last year.
Fields alleges that Emil Bove, then the acting deputy attorney general, told Akil Davis, the head of the field office to open an investigation into protesters’ activities outside federal buildings, even though Fields says the demonstrations were protected free speech, and several FBI employees in the field office expressed concern with the legality of these requests.
Field, who joined the FBI in May 2016, also alleges that Trump reportedly viewed a TikTok video of protesters in Alhambra, California that alerted neighbors about the presence of federal immigration officers and advised them of their legal rights. The White House, Fields says, then instructed Patel to direct the Los Angeles field office to initiate an investigation into those demonstrating in the video, because the president “was angry about the incident”.
Despite the fact that member of Fields’ team determined that the protesters’ actions were constitutionally protected and there was insufficient evidence, Fields was told by a colleague – whose name is redacted – that “the president wants this investigation”. Fields says that even though her supervisor acknowledged the investigation was unconstitutional, the directive still had to be followed.
Fields alleges that a “dedicated immigration squad” was created, comprising 10 agents, some of whom were taken off active cartel cases to carry out the White House’s requests. Fields says that she questioned the directives “operational logic” but her supervisor – whose name is also redacted in the complaint – described the move as “optics” designed to “make a show for the president”.
Fields says, however, she was not aware of any “actual or potential national security threat, federal criminal activity, or vulnerability” that would have warranted conducting assessments or opening investigations into anti-ICE and CBP protesters at the time.
She ultimately resigned from the bureau last year after she was removed from overseeing several programs, and believes that her diminished role was the result of objecting to protest-related investigations, according to the complaint.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called the allegations, laid out in the disclosure, “false” in a statement to the Guardian. “The first amendment does not protect violent rioting, obstructing law enforcement, and assaulting law enforcement,” she said. “Assaulting and obstructing law enforcement is a crime. This administration has been clear: anyone who assaults or obstructs law enforcement will be arrested and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
The FBI and justice department did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
In a letter to Todd Blanche, the attorney general, and Patel,
Padilla asks dozens of questions about the reported investigations, including whether they resulted in arrests, how many directives of this kind the justice department has received from the president and how many investigations are still open.

articles.title_orig: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.title_zh: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
articles.content_orig:
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.
As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.
"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."
The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.
Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.
Riot police use a water cannon as they face students during a protest against under-resourced schools, in Rennes, western France, Tuesday. Jeremias Gonzalez/AP hide caption
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.
Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."
More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.
Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."
"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.
Students chant slogans during a demonstration against under-resourced schools, in Paris, Tuesday. Teresa Suarez/AP hide caption
The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.
Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.
The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.
Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.
"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.
At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.
Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.
Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.
At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.
"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.
Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."
Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.
Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.
"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."
Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.

articles.title_orig: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.title_zh: “All things in the world must end”: Castro’s Mama Ji’s is closing at the end of the month
articles.content_orig:
Rising rent puts an end to the dim sum and Sichuan restaurant that has been in the neighborhood for almost 15 years.
Mama Ji’s (opens in new tab) in the Castro was filled with diners Monday night. Waiters bustled around, moving between the compact dining room and sidewalk tables, shuttling plates of kung pao shrimp, triple “C” wings, and hot-and-numbing fish. They told diners about the night’s special, inspired by the most recent trip Lily Ji — customers know her as Mama Ji — took to the Sichuan province of China: crispy lotus-root cake topped with minced pork in fish sauce.
Judging by how busy the restaurant was, you’d never guess it would likely be diners’ final visits. The last day of service for Mama Ji’s, which opened almost 15 years ago, is set for Oct. 31.
Ji and her husband, Marv Wolpa, posted a letter on the door sharing the news and expressing gratitude for the neighbors who have supported their mom-and-pop restaurant but saying it is time for them to put their time and energy into their personal lives. “Work is a lot; I won’t miss the work,” Ji said. “But I will miss the people.”
In an interview with The Standard, Ji gave more context to the closure: The landlord had raised the rent, citing rising insurance costs and an inability to charge more for the residential unit above Mama Ji’s. “I said, ‘Whatever that’s your decision,’” Ji said. “That’s my decision to not continue.”
The couple, who are Castro residents, started serving the food Ji grew up eating as a pop-up, then transitioned to the full restaurant in 2013. Over the decade and a half the couple served their neighborhood, Mama Ji’s became a staple of the neighborhood.
One couple dining Monday night expressed their sadness. The waiter repeated what the letter said, noting that Ji and Wolpa are ready to retire. “All things in the world must end,” he concluded as he walked away.
As for Ji, she didn’t miss a beat when asked about what she plans to do next: “Relax!”
Madeline Taub is a food reporter intern at The Standard. She was previously a contributor to Cityside’s food publication, East Bay Nosh. She graduated from UC Berkeley Graduate School of Journalism.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says intelligence shows Russia is preparing massive attack
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says intelligence shows Russia is preparing massive attack
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine says its long-range strikes have hurt Russian economy while Vladimir Putin concedes they have cost Russia roughly 1% of GDP. What we know on day 1,686
Long-range Ukrainian strikes have taken out more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity, hampering Moscow’s ability to supply its forces during the war, the defence ministry in Kyiv has claimed. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly attacked refineries from Moscow to Siberia, sparking a widespread fuel crisis in Russia earlier this year that forced authorities to restrict petrol sales. “Fifty-one per cent of struck refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, to its ability to carry out aggression and supply its troop groupings,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara said. “Our deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory.”
Russian officials have not released figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. But in a rare acknowledgment of the strikes’ economic impact , Vladimir Putin said they had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. “They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” the Russian president told a meeting of the Valdai Club forum of international foreign policy experts last Thursday.
Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries for high petrol prices, saying the Iran war was no longer responsible. “What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘Refineries,’ where Russia’s are being blown up by Ukraine,” the US president posted on his Truth Social platform.
Six people were killed and nearly 60 injured when Russian bombs struck a residential area of Ukraine’s north-eastern city of Kharkiv on Monday, officials said. Rescue workers led stunned ‌residents out of badly damaged buildings and flats, guiding them carefully around piles of rubble. Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, lies close to the Russian border and has come under regular shelling and drone attacks since Moscow invaded in February 2022. French president Emmanuel Macron condemned Russia’s decision to scale up strikes on civilian infrastructure , saying Moscow “has made the irresponsible choice to intensify its strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets”.
Russian drones struck a grain ship in the Black Sea on Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, after Romania reported a ship had caught fire and sunk near its coast with two crew members killed. “A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn,” the Ukrainian president said on X, adding that the ship was Turkish-owned and that Azerbaijani and Indian nationals were onboard. Romanian authorities said two crew members had died and 11 were rescued after the 139-metre-long (455 foot) Royad Mammadov caught fire in the Black Sea, an increasing battlefield for drone attacks in the war. War-related objects found in the Black Sea had more than doubled in six months, maritime risk expert Ambrey said last month in a report. At least a third of them carried live payloads. The objects include unexploded ordnance, drones and other unmanned vehicles found washed ashore or floating at sea, it said.
Ukrainian drones attacked two facilities at the Russian-held ⁠Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in south-eastern Ukraine overnight on Monday, but there was no threat to nuclear safety, the ⁠head of Russia’s state ⁠nuclear corporation ​said . Alexei Likhachev, director general of Rosatom, said a driver delivering food for plant employees was killed in the drone attack. According ⁠to Likhachev, a laboratory building and a radioactive waste processing plant were the targets. Ukraine has not commented on the incident.
Ukraine has begun using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to take down Russia’s new and fast-moving jet-powered drones. For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out. Presidential adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said on social media that 12 automated turrets had been installed in Kyiv to counter jet-powered Shahed drones, with more planned. Ukraine’s air force later said it had used the robotic turrets to successfully shoot down Russian jet-powered drones, including the Geran-5, for the first time. “It’s machine vision that is used for the shootdowns,” air force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Ukrainian television. “Artificial intelligence makes it possible to engage even jet-powered drones.”
Germany’s foreign intelligence chief has warned that the country risks being drawn into a conflict with Russia as hybrid attacks ordered by Moscow increase. Martin Jaeger, head of Germany’s BND spy service, told lawmakers on Monday that Russia’s undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and its allies was escalating further and has “taken on a new, more dangerous character”. Berlin has invested record sums into rebuilding its military to deter Russia, and is among the largest supporters of Ukraine in the war with Moscow. In Brussels, EU foreign policy chief ⁠Kaja Kallas said Russia ⁠was putting lives at risk across Europe with hybrid attacks.

A variant of the H1N1 influenza virus is dominating flu season in the Northern Hemisphere so far this year. Shown here are H1N1 influenza virus particles (yellow) releasing from an infected lung cell (green). Credit: Science Photo Library
Data show that flu season in the Northern Hemisphere might be off to an early start — prompting a rethink about when people should get their annual vaccines against the influenza virus . The percentage of positive tests for influenza is unusually high for this time of the year in places such as the United Kingdom and on the West Coast of the United States (see ‘Surprising start’). In Japan, outbreaks in August and early September forced some schools to close just as they were starting back up after the summer break.
“It would be an incredibly early season” for the United States if the cases researchers are seeing on the West Coast continue to rise at their current rate, says Scott Hensley, a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.
The influenza subtype responsible for most of the US cases so far is H1N1, in a flip from last year, when H3N2 dominated. And sequencing data from these early cases point to an emerging mutation in H1N1 that is causing concern among specialists.
Source: Adapted from US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data
These findings come from a relatively small number of positive tests compared with those available during peak flu season, so it’s too soon to predict the overall trajectory of the outbreak, researchers say. “An early start doesn’t necessarily mean a more severe season,” says James Hay, an epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, UK. Still, “there is something afoot”, wrote epidemiologist Caitlin Rivers in her newsletter, ‘Force of Infection’, on 27 September .
It’s enough to make Rivers, who is a researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, reconsider her personal protection strategy. In a typical year, when flu season peaks in December and January in the United States, she would wait until mid-to-late October for a shot, to get the best protection. Now, she’s thinking about getting a jab as soon as possible.
Seasonal flu is usually caused by some combination of three viruses: two subtypes of influenza A — H3N2 and H1N1 — and influenza B. Because influenza viruses genetically mutate over time and people’s immunity alters as they get vaccines and infections, which of the three viruses emerges as dominant changes for each flu season. US data showed that, during the week ending on 26 September, H1N1 accounted for 96% of positive cases for which subtyping was performed. H3N2 accounted for almost 4% of cases, and influenza B wasn’t detected.
That’s in contrast to last year, when a new variant of H3N2, called subclade K, emerged. It became globally dominant because it had many mutations that made people more vulnerable to it.

Will the mRNA flu shot work better than a regular seasonal one? What the science says
This year, the H1N1 mutation that is worrying researchers is G155E. Alex Greninger, a virologist at the University of Washington in Seattle, says that his laboratory detected G155E in 13 of 17 H1N1 samples taken from people in whom the genetic sequences were complete enough to identify specific mutations. The samples had come from hospitals and clinics in Seattle over the past few months.
This mutation had already been flagged in an analysis led by Jesse Bloom, a virologist at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, which was posted on the preprint server bioRxiv last month, ahead of peer review 1 .
Bloom and his colleagues tested how well antibodies in blood samples from 260 people in Australia and the United States were able to recognize and block infection from 148 influenza A viruses circulating by mid-2026. “We saw that a number of strains which have the G155E mutation are, in some cases, less well recognized by pre-existing human antibodies,” Bloom says. Antibodies in serum from teenagers and young adults were especially inept at recognizing this variant, probably because many in these groups haven’t been exposed to H1N1 viruses with similar characteristics before .

articles.title_orig: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.title_zh: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.content_orig:
Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director at Chanel . “I am happy with where we are at.”
Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. In Vanity Fair’s list of the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.
Blazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.
One of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featured Vanessa Paradis in a birdcage ; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.
After several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.
The same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.
after newsletter promotion
On his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”
The famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.

articles.title_orig: Brendan Carr’s ABC license fight meets a skeptical judge
articles.title_zh: Brendan Carr’s ABC license fight meets a skeptical judge
articles.content_orig:
Lawyers tell judge ABC being unfairly targeted as US regulator seeks review of network’s local TV station licenses
Lawyers for Disney accused the Trump administration of “blatant violations of the US constitution” and censorship on Tuesday in the first court hearing over the Federal Communications Commission’s early review of the media giant’s eight local television station licenses.
District judge Loren AliKhan seemed unswayed by government arguments that the order to force Disney’s ABC to apply years early to renew local television station licenses was tied to an investigation into parent company Disney’s hiring practices.
ABC, Disney and its station group filed suit against the FCC in August , seeking to block the US media regulator from taking any further steps to punish or pressure the network in connection to the order.
In its lawsuit, ABC argued that the FCC’s actions – taken at the behest of the Donald Trump-appointed chair, Brendan Carr – were actually intended to chill the network’s speech, which the president and Carr have argued is tilted against the administration.
In legal filings and during Tuesday’s hearing, the network cited past threats by the president and the FCC chairman that jeopardized the licenses of television networks, including ABC on several occasions, for editorial purposes.
“These are blatant violations of the US constitution,” the prominent trial lawyer Beth Wilkinson, arguing on behalf of ABC, told the judge during the approximately two-hour hearing.
She said ABC faced a “chilling effect” that has affected – and will continue to impact – its editorial decision-making, as the network steers clear of political bookings and any other programming decisions that could spark further ire from the Trump administration and Carr. “That chilling effect has been happening and will happen every day,” she said, causing “irreparable harm” to the network and its ability to broadcast independent news for the benefit of the American people.
ABC has said it has stopped booking politicians on the daytime talkshow The View and chose to air a July speech by Trump on its streaming platform so as not to antagonize the president. “Our editorial decisions are being affected right now,” Wilkinson said, noting the significance of decisions about how to cover next month’s pivotal midterm elections. “We are watching everything we do … We have already altered our conduct because of the fear of retaliation.”
She also noted that ABC recently chose to air a Jimmy Kimmel-conducted interview with Texas US Senate candidate James Talarico on YouTube, rather than television, “because the FCC has no control over YouTube”.
Dimitar P Georgiev, representing the FCC defendants, argued that “there is no reason to believe the early renewal order has prompted changes to the plaintiffs’ editorial decisions”. He also argued that the US district court for the District of Columbia was not the proper jurisdiction for the case, saying that ABC could instead appeal any adverse decision to the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia.
ABC is seeking a decision from the judge to enjoin the FCC from taking any further actions against the network’s licenses. “We are asking to stop pure retaliation, putting us in a process that we should never have to be in,” Wilkinson said.
In what Wilkinson called a “fatal admission”, Georgiev said the license renewal process “is not about the licenses”, but is instead a “tool” to expedite the commission’s review of ABC for potential violations of federal equal opportunities regulations. The lawyer also said the FCC could choose to end the license review process early if ABC is able to satisfy its document requests.
Considering that the FCC opened its employment practice investigation into Disney last year, with requests for documents ongoing since then, the judge asked: “Why is it only in the summer that you determined that their responses were woefully inadequate?”
She also questioned why the commission required the company to submit renewal applications for all eight of its stations simultaneously.
And she noted past comments by Carr about the network’s licenses, including a remark in July, when he had said ABC’s decision not to carry the president’s speech that month on its linear channel could factor into the license investigation.
“It strikes me with all the comments that this was merely over a discovery dispute, what made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Judge AliKhan asked lawyers for the FCC, whom she asked for a list of some of the other enforcement actions the commission could have taken short of calling up the network’s licenses early.
And she noted that there was “some daylight” in the FCC’s arguments, considering that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) inquiry was handled by the commission’s enforcement bureau, while the license order was made by the media bureau.
The judge ended the hearing without issuing an order, saying she would take the matter “under advisement”.
